cim: Mozambique’s INTIC promotes cybersecurity awareness and responsible use of artificial intelligence
cim_eredeti: Mozambique’s INTIC promotes cybersecurity awareness and responsible use of artificial intelligence
szoveg_eredeti:
Mozambique’s National Institute of Information and Communication Technologies (INTIC, IP) has conducted cybersecurity awareness activities in Matola and Maputo Province to educate students and civil servants on digital risks, social media protection and the responsible use of artificial intelligence (AI).

The activities, held on October 21 and 22 as part of Cybersecurity Awareness Month, were organised through the National Cybersecurity Incident Response Team (CSIRT Nacional) in coordination with the Provincial Social Services (SPAS) of Matola.

On October 22, awareness sessions focused on protecting social media accounts and identifying fake profiles, with participants alerted to warning signs such as perfect photos, requests for money or private content, and approaches to private conversations.

The speakers advised participants not to respond to suspicious content, to keep evidence, block and report suspicious profiles, and seek help from trusted adults. In cases of account invasion, they recommended immediately changing passwords, terminating unknown sessions, activating two-factor authentication, notifying contacts and reporting the incident to the relevant platform.

The sessions also reinforced the importance of not sharing security codes or exposing location information.

At the Industrial and Commercial Institute of Matola, the sessions were conducted by Afonso Zucula and Celson Massango, while Judas Tadeu and Vânia Zacarias led the sessions at the Institute for Training in Public and Municipal Administration (IFAPA).

On October 21, National CSIRT staff members Elves Teles and Lúcio Nhadumbuque delivered a lecture to employees of the Council of State Representation Services of Maputo Province on the dangers of the indiscriminate use of artificial intelligence in the civil service.

The session highlighted the risks of entering institutional documents into unauthorised tools, using personal accounts and accepting unverified AI-generated responses.

Employees were advised to protect personal and confidential data, prioritise authorised tools and ensure human supervision before signing documents, publishing information or making decisions. These precautions were presented as important measures to avoid fraud, information leaks, manipulation and disinformation.

The session also stressed that AI should serve as a support tool and never as an authority, ensuring that citizens’ data is not used as test material.

INTIC said the initiatives form part of its programme to strengthen digital literacy and promote safe technology practices in Mozambique.
